explanation: Transform every positive exchange rate r into −log10(r), then run Bellman–Ford from vertex 0. A further relaxation after n−1 passes identifies a negative cycle and therefore a profitable round trip.
timeComplexity: O(n³): at most n passes each relax n² exchange edges, with constant work per edge.
spaceComplexity: O(n) distances; transformed edge weights are computed as needed rather than stored in another matrix.
attribution: Adapted reference from epi_judge_python_solutions/arbitrage.py; Elements of Programming Interviews Judge contributors; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International, retained in repository LICENSE. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: Summing −log10 rates around a cycle equals −log10 of the rate product, so a profitable product greater than one is exactly a negative cycle in exact arithmetic. The complete rate matrix makes every currency reachable from 0. After n−1 full edge passes every simple path is covered; a further strict improvement therefore indicates a negative cycle, subject to floating-point roundoff.
walkthrough: With rates [[1,2],[0.6,1]], the cycle 0→1→0 has product 1.2 and transformed sum −log10(1.2)<0. Relaxing its edges lowers a distance again after the first pass, so the extra scan returns true.
edgeCases: All rates must be finite and strictly positive for logarithms.
An exactly neutral cycle has product one and is not profitable mathematically.
This version uses strict floating-point comparisons with no epsilon, so near-neutral products can be affected by roundoff.
An empty rate matrix returns false.
